book_title: Following the Capital Trail: Warrants, EMS, and Promoter Sales
question: How has management allocated raised capital across capex, JVs, and working capital—and what do promoter stake sales and SME governance disclosures reveal?

epigraph.quote: Show me the cash-flow statement and the shareholding pattern, and I will tell you what management truly believes.
epigraph.author: Capital Allocation Principle

web_blocks.html: Kody Technolab is led by founder, Chairman, and MD Manav Subhashchandra Patel alongside CEO Sanjay Kidecha [3]. Promoter group members Manali Krunal Patel and Pooja Sunny Patel also sit on the cap table [3]. Judging this team means looking past launch events. We must read the capital trail inside the FY25–H1 FY27 balance sheets and exchange filings.

web_blocks.title: Capital-Raising Cadence: Preferential Warrants, Debt, and Promoter Credit Lines

web_blocks.html: Between March 2025 and September 2026, Kody raised and spent capital at a rapid clip. Equity Capital plus Reserves nearly tripled from ₹79 Cr (Mar 2025) to ₹215 Cr (Mar 2026) and ₹229 Cr (Sep 2026) [1]. That surge came from +₹113 Cr of Financing Cash Flow in FY26 via preferential shares and convertible warrants (25% upfront, 75% on conversion) [1, 4]. In H1 FY27, warrant conversions added over ₹10 Cr more [7]. Yet external debt still jumped over threefold from ₹8 Cr (Mar 2026) to ₹27 Cr (Sep 2026) [1]. The board also cleared up to ₹100 Cr in unsecured promoter credit lines for working capital [7].

web_blocks.caption: Capital Allocation & Ownership Scorecard (Mar 2025 – Oct 2026)
rows: Massive equity infusion via preferential shares & convertible warrants [1, 4].
5.7x asset buildout for robotics fleets, R&D, and EMS integration [1].
Debt re-accelerated +₹19 Cr in 6 months alongside ₹100 Cr promoter credit approval [1, 7].
Zero cash returned to minority shareholders; 100% retained for capex & working capital [1].
Down -419 bps from Sep 2025 (73.01%) via dilution & MD open-market sales [1, 4].
Small retail/HNI float; negligible FII (0.09%) and DII (0.16%) institutional ownership [1].
web_blocks.takeaway: Management deployed ₹130+ Cr of fresh equity and debt into fixed assets and working capital over 18 months. Over the same span, promoter stake fell 4.19 percentage points and institutional ownership stayed under 0.3%.

web_blocks.html: Two governance points stand out. First, promoter holding sat at 73.01% from September 2023 through September 2025 [1]. It then fell to 72.73% (Mar 2026), 69.49% (Sep 2026), and 68.82% (Oct 2026) [1]. Automated screens flagged a -3.91% quarterly drop [1]. Warrant conversions diluted the base, and MD Manav Subhashchandra Patel also sold shares in open-market and bulk deals [4]. Trimming founder stock during a cash-burning pivot sends a mixed signal.

Second, Kody now spans a wider web of group entities. These include World EMS Private Limited, Kody Media Limited, Kody Middle East Holding LLC, and Falcon Tech Robotics LLC [6, 7]. Management filed SEBI LODR notes stating that deals like World EMS are judged at arm's length [7]. Even so, NSE Emerge SME companies report full accounts half-yearly rather than quarterly. Minority holders therefore get less frequent visibility into inter-company cash flows.

web_blocks.title: Why Capital Intensity Tests SME Governance

web_blocks.html: Asset-light IT firms leave little room for cash to hide. Once an SME builds factories, RaaS fleets, and overseas JVs, governance risk rises fast. Investors should track three items over the next two half-years. First, watch if Kody draws the ₹100 Cr unsecured promoter credit line and at what interest rate [7]. Second, check if billing across World EMS, Kody Media, and Falcon Tech turns into real consolidated cash flow [1, 6, 7]. Third, verify whether promoter stake holds steady near 68.8% without fresh sales [1, 4].

Shareholder mix adds another clue. Between September 2025 and October 2026, total shareholders fell from 3,430 to 2,704 [1]. Combined FII and DII ownership stayed tiny at 0.25% [1]. Kody's expanded equity sits mostly with promoters and non-promoter warrant holders rather than large institutional funds. Zero dividend payouts in FY25 and FY26 confirm that all profits stay inside the business [1]. Until institutional funds enter the register, external governance oversight remains limited [1].

web_blocks.title: Governance Watchlist: Institutional Absence & Other Income
paragraphs: Combined FII (0.09%) and DII (0.16%) ownership is just 0.25% as of October 2026 [1]. Meanwhile, Other Income climbed to ₹7 Cr in FY26 (27% of PBT) and ₹9.21 Cr TTM (32% of PBT) [1]. Until institutional funds enter and core cash flow replaces treasury yield, governance remains a show-me item.

book_paragraphs: When a company is growing its top line at nearly 100% year-on-year, management interviews always sound visionary. To stay grounded, you and I have to mute the audio and audit two quiet documents: the cash-flow statement and the shareholding table. Together, they tell the story of how Kody Technolab's leadership actually allocates capital.

Over the eighteen months between March 2025 and September 2026, Manav Patel and his team pulled in massive amounts of outside capital. Equity capital and reserves leaped from ₹79 crore to ₹229 crore, fueled by ₹113 crore of financing cash inflows in FY26 from preferential share allotments and convertible warrants. Then, in the first half of FY27, external borrowings jumped more than threefold from ₹8 crore to ₹27 crore, and the board cleared an additional ₹100 crore unsecured promoter funding line.

Where did all that money go? Roughly ₹71 crore went into fixed assets and capital work-in-progress, which swelled from ₹15 crore to ₹86 crore as Kody built out its robot fleets, R&D facilities, and manufacturing tie-up with World EMS Private Limited. Another large chunk went into financing 197 days of working capital and 192 days of customer receivables. Meanwhile, ₹34 to ₹36 crore sat in investments, generating ₹7 crore of Other Income in FY26 and ₹9.21 crore over the trailing twelve months—accounting for nearly a third of pre-tax profits.

Now look at the shareholding column, because this is where alignment gets nuanced. From the September 2023 IPO right through September 2025, promoters held an unchanged 73.01%. Over the following year, that stake slid to 68.82% by October 2026. Part of the drop was mechanical dilution from non-promoter warrant conversions, which is normal when raising growth equity. Part of it, however, came from open-market and bulk-deal share sales by Managing Director Manav Patel himself. When a founder trims personal equity at the exact moment the company is borrowing more and asking non-promoter investors to fund negative free cash flow, you and I are right to ask tough questions.

Add to that the structural reality of an NSE Emerge SME listing. Kody reports full financial results only half-yearly rather than quarterly, carries just 0.25% combined FII and DII ownership, and now operates through multiple domestic and UAE entities—Kody Media, Kody Middle East, Falcon Tech Robotics, and World EMS. None of this proves wrongdoing, and management has disclosed arm's-length evaluations under SEBI rules. But it does mean Kody is still a 'trust-but-verify' governance story rather than an institutional-grade compounder.

Consider what happens when a high-growth SME relies on preferential warrants and promoter credit lines simultaneously. Preferential warrants—where non-promoter investors pay 25% upfront and 75% upon conversion—bring in equity without immediate cash-flow strain, and Kody's reserves swelled from ₹66 crore to ₹215 crore as a result. Yet despite that ₹149 crore jump in reserves, by September 2026 the company still needed to triple its external borrowings from ₹8 crore to ₹27 crore and authorize up to ₹100 crore of unsecured promoter funding.

Why would a company that just raised over ₹113 crore in FY26 financing inflows need ₹27 crore of debt and a ₹100 crore promoter credit backstop six months later? The answer lies in the sheer speed of asset and working-capital absorption: ₹86 crore locked in fixed assets, ₹34 crore in investments, and ₹177 crore in other assets including 192-day receivables. That is a textbook capital-allocation stress test. If those deployed assets start throwing off strong operating cash in FY27 and FY28, management's bold balance-sheet bet will look prescient. If receivables keep swelling while debt climbs, minority shareholders face the twin risks of further equity dilution and rising interest drag.

There is also a subtle signal in the shareholder count. Between September 2025 and October 2026, total shareholders fell from 3,430 to 2,704 while promoter holding declined and institutional ownership stayed negligible at 0.25%. That means the company's expanded equity base is concentrated among a relatively small pool of high-net-worth and non-promoter warrant holders rather than broad institutional funds. Watching whether marquee domestic or foreign institutions step onto the register over the next year will be an important external validation test.

At the same time, zero dividend payouts—0% across FY25 and FY26 despite reported profits—confirm that every rupee of internal cash is being retained to feed the balance sheet. Retaining 100% of earnings is fine when incremental returns on capital exceed 20%. When working capital days sit at 197 and ROE sits at 11.4%, however, minority shareholders deserve crystal-clear proof that retained capital is compounding rather than plugging cash leaks.

That is why the board's ₹100 crore unsecured promoter funding approval is a double-edged sword. On one hand, it shows the founders are willing to backstop liquidity if bank credit tightens. On the other hand, needing a ₹100 crore credit line right after raising ₹113 crore in equity signals that working capital is consuming cash faster than operations generate it.

book_callouts.title: The Alignment Check
book_callouts.text: Watch three governance needles over the next two half-years: whether promoter shareholding stabilizes above 68%, whether the ₹100 Cr unsecured promoter credit line is drawn at arm's-length terms, and whether World EMS and Falcon Tech transactions translate into consolidated CFO rather than standalone profits.
